newsitem.title: GERMANY: Demirel tells Kohl Turkey has to defend itself.
newsitem.headline: Demirel tells Kohl Turkey has to defend itself.

text.p: Turkish President Suleyman Demirel told German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Tuesday his country had to defend itself against separatism and would continue to do so, a Bonn government spokesman said.
Outside the chancellery where Kohl and Demirel met, some 200 people demonstrated against Turkey's human rights policies.

Demirel told Kohl his country "had to and would continue to defend itself against separatist tendencies" and emphasised that Turkey was a secular, democratic country with a market economy which respected human rights, a Bonn official statement said.

Demirel's four-day state visit to Germany began on Monday in Berlin where he ran into several hundred protesters demonstrating against alleged human rights violations against separatist Kurds in Turkey.
He was protected by a tight security cordon during his visit to Bonn where he also met other German political leaders.
Several Kurdish groups have spoken out against his visit.

"Demirel's policies stand for the suppression of the Kurdish people," said Mehmet Tanriverdi, chairman of the Kurdish community in Germany. "The German government should immediately break off its economic and military support for Turkey."

The association of Kurdish groups (KOMKAR) said in a statement that Demirel had held high offices in Turkey for 30 years and was "primarily responsible for the permanent and systematic human rights violations in Turkey".

In Berlin on Monday a group of about 150 demonstrators, led by Amnesty International, booed and whistled as Demirel entered the city hall. Police struggled with demonstrators and several were detained.
Security was tight because of police concerns there might be disturbances from the outlawed Kurdish Workers Party (PKK). Police and the PKK have clashed several times in recent years.
Around 2.2 million Turkish citizens live in Germany, the largest foreign community in the country and just under a third of the total immigrant population.
Turks were the prime targets of a three-year wave of racist and neo-Nazi violence that followed German unification in 1990.
The attacks, carried out by right-wing extremists, subsided but Turkish properties have been the target of firebombings by the PKK which is fighting for autonomy in southeastern Turkey.

The European parliament, angered by Turkey's human rights record, voted in a first reading of the 1997 European Union budget last month to block hundreds of millions of dollars of aid to help Ankara set up a customs union with the EU.
